newsitem.title: UK: British farmer income at new peak - accountants.
newsitem.headline: British farmer income at new peak - accountants.

text.p: High world prices for grains and potatoes and European Union (EU) aid payments combined to make 1995/96 the most profitable year ever for British farmers, according to chartered accountants Deloitte & Touche.
But this combination is unlikely to be repeated and the firm said farmers must plan for leaner times and expect much more volatile markets as trade barriers are reduced.
The survey of farm incomes is based on the actual returns from the 83,000 hectares farmed by Deloitte & Touche's Agriculture's clients in lowland England.
Average land use was 62 percent combinable crops, eight percent root crops, 14 percent for forage/dairy with nine percent in set-aside.
The survey shows average net income in the year to end-June 1996 rose 29 percent to 363 stg a hectare, said Deloitte partner Vincent Hedley Lewis.

But there was a wide gap between the most and least profitable farmers with the top 25 percent seeing net income rising 20 percent to 717 stg a hectare whilst for the bottom quartile it climbed 82 stg to just 104 stg a hectare.
Most of the improvements came from a sharp improvement in combinable crops and were due to factors beyond farmers' control like weather, world trade, exchange rates and to a lesser extent EU policy.
Deloitte said the best farmers made the most efficient use of inputs.

The top 25 percent had the highest wheat yeilds of 8.28 tonne per hectare and thanks to tight cost controls including spending less than the average on sprays, had the lowest production costs per tonne of 79 stg.
The lowest quartile of Deloitte's clients achieved a wheat yield of 7.78 tonnes a hectare at a cost of 99 stg a tonne.
Farm size, soil types and the amount spent on variable costs were not significant factors in differentiating between farmers' profitability.
